title: Ride-Hailing Dispatch Platform
summary: Design the backend of a ride-hailing app: ingest live driver locations, match riders with nearby drivers within seconds, and run the trip lifecycle reliably across many cities.
statement:
You are designing the core backend of **a ride-hailing app** operating in about 100 cities on several continents.

**Drivers**
- Go online and offline. While online (and during trips) the driver app reports its GPS position every 4 seconds.
- Receive ride offers ("pickup 1.2 km away, 6 min") and accept or decline each within 15 seconds.
- Move the trip forward: arrived at pickup → trip started → trip completed. Drivers can cancel before pickup.

**Riders**
- Open the app and see available cars moving on the map around them.
- Enter a destination, see an upfront fare and a pickup ETA, and request a ride.
- Get matched with a driver, watch the driver approach on the map and follow the trip live.
- Can cancel before pickup (a fee applies after 2 minutes) and receive a receipt with the route after the trip.

**Clarifications from the interviewer**
- Matching should prefer the driver with the shortest *driving* time to the pickup, not just the nearest in a straight line. If the offered driver declines or doesn't answer, the next best driver is tried, for up to 3 minutes in total before the rider is told no cars are available.
- A pricing component (fare plus any surge multiplier for an area) and a maps component (routes and ETAs) already exist; treat them as dependencies you call.
- Demand is spiky and very local: a concert ending can produce thousands of requests within a few square kilometres in minutes.
- Mobile connectivity is unreliable; apps may disconnect for tens of seconds and reconnect.
- Trips are local to a city; nobody needs to see drivers from another city.

Cover requirements, estimates, API, data model and architecture, then go deep on location handling, matching and keeping trips consistent.
scaleHints: 5M registered drivers; up to 1.5M online simultaneously at the global peak
Location updates every 4 s from online drivers → ~375K updates/s at peak (~100 bytes each)
~20M completed trips per day (~230/s on average); ride requests peak at ~1K/s globally, with single-city hotspots of ~200/s
Rider sees a matched driver within 10 s at p95; positions on the map refresh every 4–5 s
Completed-trip routes kept 2 years for receipts and disputes; idle-driver pings need not be kept beyond 24 hours
constraints: A driver must never be assigned two active trips, and a ride request must never be matched to two drivers
In-progress trips must survive server failures (99.99% availability for the trip lifecycle)
Driver positions used for matching must be at most ~10 s old; drivers who stopped reporting must not receive offers
Location data is personal data: access is restricted and regional retention limits apply
outOfScope: Payment processing, driver payouts and tipping
Pricing/surge algorithms and routing/ETA engine internals (both are given dependencies)
Pooled or scheduled rides and food delivery
Driver onboarding, ratings and support tooling

keyFunctionalRequirements: Driver online/offline status and continuous location ingestion
Show nearby available drivers to riders on a map
Fare and ETA estimate, then ride request
Dispatch: rank candidates by ETA, send offers with a 15 s timeout, try the next driver, give up after 3 min
Trip state machine: requested → matched → driver arriving → in progress → completed / cancelled
Live trip tracking for the rider and a receipt with the route
keyNonFunctionalRequirements: Ingest ~375K location updates/s into a queryable live index with low latency
Match within 10 s at p95; nearby-driver queries in tens of milliseconds
Strong consistency for assignments (no double booking) while locations can be eventually consistent
99.99% availability for in-flight trips; tolerate client disconnects
Geographic partitioning by city/region and handling of local hotspots
coreEntities: Driver: driver_id, vehicle, status (offline/available/offered/on_trip), current_trip_id, city
DriverLocation (live, ephemeral): driver_id, lat, lng, heading, cell_id, updated_at
RideRequest: request_id, rider_id, pickup, dropoff, fare_quote_id, status, created_at
Trip: trip_id, rider_id, driver_id, state, per-state timestamps, fare, route_ref, version
DispatchOffer: offer_id, request_id, driver_id, sent_at, expires_at, response
keyComponents: Location ingestion service accepting high-rate driver pings over persistent connections
In-memory geospatial index of available drivers (geohash/H3/S2 cells or quadtree), partitioned by city
Dispatch/matching service that queries candidates, calls the ETA service and reserves a driver atomically
Trip service owning the trip state machine with durable storage and idempotent transitions
Real-time push channel to rider and driver apps (offers, positions, trip updates)
Pricing and maps/ETA dependencies, with caching of area-level results
Location history pipeline writing trip routes to cheap durable storage
deepDiveTopics: Geospatial indexing at 375K updates/s: cell size trade-offs, searching neighbouring cells/rings, partitioning by city
Preventing double assignment: compare-and-set or a lease on the driver that expires with the offer timeout
Dispatch strategy: greedy best-ETA vs batching requests over a short window; handling declines and timeouts
Hotspots (stadiums, airports): splitting hot cells, queueing requests, protecting the ETA dependency
Durable, idempotent trip state transitions under retries and app reconnects
Stale or disconnected drivers: heartbeat TTLs and eviction from the live index
commonPitfalls: Writing every location ping synchronously to a relational database with a spatial index
Matching on straight-line distance only, ignoring the road network
No reservation or locking, so two requests grab the same driver
Clients polling for match status and driver position
One global matching service/index instead of partitioning by geography
Searching only the rider's own cell and missing drivers just across a cell boundary
